title: Shahrbanoo Sadat and Jelena Maksimović Hit Back at Discrimination in Film Funding at Tokyo Festival Talk
description: A lack of funding, and ignorance in the institutions that control it, keeps women at an inherent disadvantage in the film industry, Afghan director
body:
A lack of funding, and ignorance in the institutions that control it, keeps women at an inherent disadvantage in the film industry, Afghan director Shahrbanoo Sadat said at a Tokyo International Film Festival talk on the future of women’s cinema.

	“The discrimination did not start at the festival, but it started at the development level,” said Sadat, who sat on this year’s Venice competition jury, reflecting on the lackluster ratio of films by women selected for competition.
	

	The talk, part of the festival’s Tokyo Talk sessions at the TIFF Lounge in Tokyo Midtown Hibiya, also featured Serbian director Jelena Maksimović, whose “Until the Day Ends” played in Venice’s Orizzonti section. Sadat, now based in Germany, saw her latest feature “No Good Men” open the 76th Berlinale before screening in Tokyo. Film scholar and presenter Takasaki Ikuko moderated.

	The session followed other reflections on women’s careers in film at the festival, both in its Women’s Empowerment section and at an animation symposium held earlier the same day on the past, present and future of four women working as directors in the anime industry.

	The panel set out to discuss how women and feminism are presented in Sadat’s and Maksimović’s films and beyond, but it turned mostly to the practical, financial barriers standing in the way of more films directed by women.

	Both filmmakers said getting the means to make a film often requires a certain conformity.

	“It was also like that back in Yugoslavia,” Maksimović said, “even though it was a very progressive country there were a lot more male directors […] but things started changing in the Balkans after the Yugoslav Wars… not because of that, but because we moved into more progressive times.”
	

	There are external factors too, such as where the money for film funds comes from. Maksimović said Film Center Serbia “worked decently” for a few years, until the outgoing government cut off its funding entirely in retaliation for filmmakers’ frequent support of the student anti-corruption protests.

	The student-led movement, which grew out of protests over the deadly 2024 collapse of a train station canopy in Novi Sad, won Serbia’s snap parliamentary election on Oct. 25. Aleksandar Vučić had resigned as president in September.

	“Luckily, a few days ago the students won. We’re very happy at the moment, but there’s a huge fight in front of us,” Maksimović said, adding that the damage done by the previous regime would take time to repair.

	“Even when the film center worked normally we had a difficult time financing our films, the amount of money for Serbian films is very small and it’s hard to find co-production countries,” she said. These weren’t definitive reasons for the scarcity of Serbian films playing in Japan, she added, but male filmmakers in the country had enjoyed a privilege that women didn’t have.

	Later, Maksimović returned to the topic, saying there is a certain solidarity among filmmakers making less mainstream features, but that it’s also a “certain kind of bubble,” one separate from what she called “big funding.”

	“We didn’t dare to apply to the big funding to get more money for our films because we knew we wouldn’t get the money there,” she said. She hopes the student movement’s victory gives the system a chance to be overhauled. “I’m very proud that I’m coming from Serbia today because students really showed us that it’s possible,” she said.

	Sadat also spoke about the forces limiting filmmaking in Afghanistan.

	“There is this cultural mafia, a bunch of old men, and you as a woman, you never can get in,” she said. Getting even a slight chance at the same privileges, she added, takes capitulation, submission and compromise.

	“It’s either that to get into this network [or] community of cinema, or like what I did, get connected to another system. In my case, it was European filmmaking,” Sadat said.

	That system still has its inequalities, Sadat said. “Filmmaking in Afghanistan is a crime – it’s not as extreme as that – but the discrimination is fundamental, it’s in the system,” she added of the European funds.
	

	She said the gender gap in funding is “treated so normally,” and that a lack of proper development support and equal treatment is why there were so few films by women in competition at Venice this year. Only one of the 20 films in the Venice competition, May el-Toukhy’s “Woman Unknown,” was directed by a woman.

	Toward the end of the talk, an audience member asked how to bring about material change rather than lip service, noting that there were “only about four films in the selection made by women” at the Tokyo International Film Festival. Sadat answered by returning to Venice.

	“I was part of the Venice Film Festival this year in the main competition, and I was very surprised. I don’t want to comment on any specific film, but there were films that were just bad, but they are made by male directors. But women directors are not allowed to make bad [films],” she said. “The director of Venice, he commented when the press asked why there’s no films by women, he said, ‘Well, the quality of the films that female directors make are not good enough for competition.’”

	Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera told Variety in July that the competition’s one film directed by a woman was “the only one we found of adequate quality to compete internationally.” “Woman Unknown” went on to win Venice’s top prize, the Golden Lion.

	Sadat suggested the men did not receive the same scrutiny. Setting aside any gendered reactions, she added, filmmakers are human and there should be room for experimentation, and women are held to a higher standard where anything less than perfection is punished.

	“We have to change the systems – start with the fundings, the committees,” Maksimović said. She added that she doesn’t want her films to be considered in a tokenistic way.

	“I know people are trying to change things, but are they really changing? Or are they just putting things into boxes?” she said.

	Asked about the future, Sadat said: “Coming from a war country, and in our country, people are absolutely in survival mode. We do not think of the future; we think about the present. Change can start from little things. I don’t think that we should wait for the bigger changes, they happen like little by little, over the course of a really long time.”

schema.headline: Shahrbanoo Sadat and Jelena Maksimović Hit Back at Discrimination in Film Funding at Tokyo Festival Talk

title: Dustin Hoffman Says Filming ‘The Graduate’ Was a ‘Terrible Experience’ and Director Mike Nichols Made Katharine Ross Slap Him 27 Times for a Scene He ‘Didn’t Even Use’
description: Dustin Hoffman, who shot to fame after starring as Ben Braddock in Mike Nichols’ classic film “The Graduate,” has opened up about his experience sh
body:
Dustin Hoffman, who shot to fame after starring as Ben Braddock in Mike Nichols’ classic film “The Graduate,” has opened up about his experience shooting the 1967 comedy-drama in a recent essay for The New Yorker, which he described as having been a “terrible experience” despite the fact that the movie changed his life.

	“I felt immediately uncomfortable, unworthy. Here I was, playing a starring role in a movie by Mike Nichols, who was the director of the moment, but I felt like I had no right to be there,” writes Hoffman early in the piece of his time on set. “It was a terrible experience making the movie that changed my life.” Much of his anxiety stemmed from worrying that Nichols “was angry at me, either because I was doing something wrong or because he had realized what everybody else already knew, that he had miscast the lead in his film.”
	

	Hoffman writes that the film “exacerbated all my insecurities from the start.” “When my agent said that Mike was interested in me, I didn’t even want to try out for the part. I had read the Charles Webb novel that Mike was adapting, and it was obvious that I was all wrong for Benjamin. A track star and straight-A student, the head of the debate team—this was an affluent, all-American kid, whose surname was ‘Braddock.’ Why would you cast a person who looks as ethnic as I do to play the ultimate Wasp? It made absolutely no sense.” He continued, explaining that his agent convinced him to screen-test for the role, which he ultimately got.

	However, beyond Hoffman’s worries about his ability to play Ben, he also writes that Nichols was “frequently sour” on set, a “shocking, destabilizing” change from his personality during rehearsals. “I often felt that I was about to be fired. When we were shooting some of the film’s most famous sequences, I remember thinking, I have no fucking idea what I’m doing,” said Hoffman.
	

	He also notes that while the director was “irritable with everyone,” there was a “certain sadism” that “seemed to creep in” only with him. 

	He continued: “There was a scene in which Katharine Ross had to slap me, and he made us do twenty-seven takes. The scene has Benjamin run into Elaine’s room, soaking wet from the rain, to tell her that he’s had an affair with an older woman; within seconds, Elaine realizes the woman is her mother. Mike just kept telling Katharine to hit me, to hit me harder. Katharine worried she would hurt me, and I told her, ‘I’m O.K. Just don’t hit my ear.’ Unfortunately, she missed a few times. I was dizzy by the end of that day, and Mike didn’t even use the slap in the film.”

	The following day, Hoffman shot an underwater scene that required him to stay submerged in a scuba suit. “When I came up for air after a few takes, there was blood trickling out of my ear. Between all the slapping during the previous day and all the water pressure at the bottom of the pool, I’d punctured an eardrum,” he writes.

	“The Graduate” first hit theaters on Dec. 22, 1967. Per its official description, the film followed a disillusioned college graduate (Hoffman) who finds himself torn between his older lover (Anne Bancroft) and her daughter (Ross). It was nominated for seven Oscars and was named the best picture winner at the 40th Academy Awards.

schema.headline: Dustin Hoffman Says Filming ‘The Graduate’ Was a ‘Terrible Experience’ and Director Mike Nichols Made Katharine Ross Slap Him 27 Times for a Scene He ‘Didn’t Even Use’

title: Marty Erlichman, Longtime Manager for Barbra Streisand, Dies at 97
description: Marty Erlichman, the entertainment manager who discovered Barbra Streisand and managed her for more than six decades, died on Saturday of age-relat
body:
Marty Erlichman, the entertainment manager who discovered Barbra Streisand and managed her for more than six decades, died on Saturday of age-related causes. He was 97.

	“To the world, he was a giant of Hollywood; to us, he was a deeply devoted and loving father, husband, grandfather, and rock,” Erlichman’s family wrote in a statement. “We feel his loss deeply but are endlessly proud of the life he lived and the indelible mark he left on the world.”
	

	Over 60 years, Erlichman shaped Streisand’s career from New York nightclub singer to international star on stage and screen. He negotiated agreements and oversaw her career’s business side. He worked on her 2000 Millennium Concert, the 2006 to 2007 world tour, and executive produced her 1994 HBO special “Barbra: The Concert.”

	“Although Marty lived a long and full life, nothing can prepare you for the reality of losing someone so dear,” Streisand said in a statement. “I truly thought he would live forever. In my eyes, he was simply indestructible—always by my side, through everything. He can never be replaced, and I will be forever grateful for his friendship, loyalty, and unwavering support.”

	One of Erlichman’s other early successes in the entertainment business was as manager to the Irish folk group The Clancy Brothers and Tommy Makem. His other clients included heavyweight boxing champion George Foreman, record producer and songwriter Bob Crewe, 1960s pop group Gary Puckett & the Union Gap and comedian and actor Chevy Chase.

	Erlichman also worked as a film producer. His credits include Streisand’s 1974 comedy “For Pete’s Sake,” the 1978 psychological thriller “Coma” directed by Michael Crichton and the 1983 romantic thriller “Breathless,” starring Richard Gere.
	

	Erlichman was born Sept. 13, 1929, in Brooklyn, New York. He graduate from Drake University in Des Moines, Iowa. 

	He is survived by his wife, Miko Mayama Erlichman; their son, J.J.; daughter-in-law, Talia; and four grandchildren. Donations can be made to St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital or the National Kidney Foundation.

title: Japanese Drifter’s Road Trip to Korea Drives Uchiyama Takuya’s ‘The Blue Breaks’ at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
description: A man conceived through sperm donation, unsure of his place in the world, sets out on a journey to Korea in “The Blue Breaks,” an adaptation of Mac
body:
A man conceived through sperm donation, unsure of his place in the world, sets out on a journey to Korea in “The Blue Breaks,” an adaptation of Machiya Ryohei’s 2016 novel by Japanese filmmaker Uchiyama Takuya (“Numb”). The Japan-Italy co-production was among the projects at this year’s Tokyo Gap-Financing Market.

	The protagonist, Shukichi, is a rootless part-time worker in his thirties living at Japan’s western edge. His sense of detachment grows when he discovers that his girlfriend, with whom he lives, has a son she no longer has custody of. A night spent with a solitary boxer of Korean descent then throws his sense of identity and sexuality into further confusion.
	

	He later meets Toko, a young woman who is terminally ill but carries herself lightly, smoking and smiling despite the little time she has left. Her outlook gradually leaves its mark on him. Eventually Shukichi and the people around him travel to Korea together, where they reckon with one another’s lives and deaths.

	Uchiyama, who has previously written his own screenplays from personal experience, said he felt drawn to the book in part because it was published in the year he started making films, and because Machiya wrote it at the age Uchiyama is now.

	“Shukichi, the protagonist, struggles with the part of himself that never quite became ‘manly.’ I’ve also spent much of my life feeling uncomfortable with what society expects a man to be,” Uchiyama said.

	He described the characters as people whose lives look very different from one another’s, and said Japan still expects everyone to be alike.
	

	“Diversity isn’t something new. It’s always been there, even if we haven’t always acknowledged it,” Uchiyama said. “I wanted to approach these feelings with a sense of lightness, and to make a film about love that is unapologetically romantic.”

	Japanese producer Satoh Naomi of Differentia is behind the project, with Parsifal Reparato of Italian company Antropica as co-producer. The team is working on the screenplay, casting and financing, with a shoot planned for 2027 and completion in 2028, and is targeting a premiere at an international festival.

	Satoh said the two connected over a shared sense of not fitting the roles expected of them, whether in society at large or within the film business, and that films that resist categories can be hard to finance in Japan.

	“When ‘Numb’ was selected for the Berlinale, it gave me real proof that Takuya’s work could resonate with audiences beyond Japan,” Satoh said.

	In Tokyo, the producers made headway on the remaining financing and find international co-production partners, sales agents and distributors who could take the film beyond Japan and Italy.

	Reparato said the film’s appeal lies in how it rethinks family and identity, and that Antropica, which has been active in Asia for years, including in Vietnam, sees the project as a way to deepen ties with Japanese cinema, helped by Italy and Japan’s bilateral co-production framework.

	“At this historical moment, building bridges is more important than ever,” Reparato said.

	Uchiyama has also wrapped shooting on a separate project, which is now moving into editing.

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market ran as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

schema.headline: Japanese Drifter’s Road Trip to Korea Drives Uchiyama Takuya’s ‘The Blue Breaks’ at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market

title: ‘Between Us’ Director Matsumura Shingo on Finding Connection After Disaster and Making Films on Japanese Budgets
description: Unspoken emotional wounds linger throughout “Between Us,” Japanese director Matsumura Shingo’s new film playing in the Tokyo International Film Fes
body:
Unspoken emotional wounds linger throughout “Between Us,” Japanese director Matsumura Shingo’s new film playing in the Tokyo International Film Festival’s Nippon Cinema Now section, its strand for Japanese films.

	The film follows Makoto and Kasumi, childhood best friends who drift apart after an incident on a joint family camping trip and reunite six years later in their high school drama club. Kawashima Ririka, Kurasawa Anna, Kikuchi Akiko, Usuda Asami, Saito Yoichiro and Miura Takahiro star. The script leaves a lot unsaid, letting patient camerawork absorb the emotional information each character tries to withhold.
	

	Matsumura, whose credits include “The Lump in My Heart” (2023), favors very still camera movement and deliberate observation. He has set himself a rule against using handheld camerawork in his films.

	“All the cameras are becoming all compact right now, and you see all these videos shown on YouTube and social media that are shot by those cameras,” he says. “And so I wanted to differentiate what I show on the big screen with that kind of content. That is one of the reasons why. The second reason is that I want to capture the emotion of the actors truthfully, slowly.”

	There’s a fascinating contrast in how “Between Us” seeks emotional realism but finds it through very measured, precise camerawork, particularly in how it turns the emotional distance between Makoto and Kasumi into literal distance through the blocking of each scene.

	“What was more difficult to portray was [that] though they are apart, they are feeling the existence of the other,” Matsumura says, “and I wanted to show that with the use of the eyes and use of the space: though there was a physical space [between them], they kind of had each other in mind, and I wanted to express that through other elements.”
	

	The drama club has lost members because Kasumi takes it so seriously that others feel they can’t keep up. Even after Makoto joins the club, the two are often shot far apart, but Matsumura shows the mending through a rather simple editing decision: cutting the girls’ separate read-throughs as though they are trading lines, with each cut bringing them closer than ever before, even though they aren’t in the same room.

	“The play is a fiction, but they are speaking in their own language,” he says. “And by saying their lines, they are able to say what they were not able to say in the real world, and by doing that, their distance becomes closer.”

	The script Kasumi discovers, which gives the film its title, becomes what begins to mend their relationship, quite literally bringing them closer together.

	The intimate story has big-picture beginnings. Matsumura found inspiration in a run of disasters, starting with the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake.

	“There was the pandemic. There is the war going on around the world, and [it] was a period in my life when I thought it is impossible for one to connect with others,” he says. “So I just wanted to make a very simple film with two people, two human beings facing the other way, and to make them look at each other, and [ask] what kind of energy is born from that?”

	The story has nothing to do with those events in a literal sense, Matsumura says. What ties them to the past trauma linking Makoto and Kasumi’s families is that both are “unresolved.”

	“I think that reflects the current situation where the earthquake, the nuclear power plant, the war, if it’s on the media, we look into it. But once it’s not on the news, we feel that it’s kind of in the past solved, but it’s really not in reality,” he says.

	With his two leads, “there was no specific direction that I gave them,” Matsumura says. “This is a characteristic that they have as an actress – it’s a common characteristic – but they have interest in others, and they listen to others closely, and they take in their words and make it their own, and they have this trait. It was very natural for them to actually perform these two characters, and I just let them freely perform what they felt like.”
	

	Matsumura’s visually organized approach, paired with naturalistic performances, makes for a striking result, one that also shows the range of styles across this year’s Nippon Cinema Now lineup.

	“There is really no [singular] mainstream in the Japanese cinema now,” Matsumura says. “But one thing that is common is that the financing, the budget that we have for one film is very limited in Japan – it’s not like in the U.S. And because of that, there is a limit to what we can portray, the concept that we can portray in one film.”

	That isn’t always a negative thing, he adds. “We are all trying to make a film about a subject that is within our reach, but we’re not reaching for all the same things. We’re reaching for all different things, and that is the current Japanese cinema environment. So we’re not making a film about one big subject. Each of us are all making films about [a] variety of small subjects.”

	Matsumura says he is at a crossroads himself. “I could follow my instinct and make an artistic film, and express what is inside of me, or I could make a film for the mass audience – I won’t be facing with myself, but I’ll be facing more towards society or the audience that watches the film,” he says. “I don’t know which way I’ll go, as of now.”

schema.headline: ‘Between Us’ Director Matsumura Shingo on Finding Connection After Disaster and Making Films on Japanese Budgets

title: Jakarta World Cinema Plans to Revive First Feature Competition With International Jury
description: Jakarta World Cinema aims to bring back its First Feature Competition next year, open to filmmakers from around the world and judged by an internat
body:
Jakarta World Cinema aims to bring back its First Feature Competition next year, open to filmmakers from around the world and judged by an international jury.

	This year’s edition did not accept submissions. The competition was put on hold because of the difficulty of assembling an international jury.

	“[Previously] we’ve only had Indonesian judges,” festival director Shandy Gasella tells Variety.


	Next year, the team wants to bring in international jury members with strong filmographies, so the category can open to submissions from filmmakers worldwide.
	

	The festival sits between October’s Jakarta Film Week and the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival at the end of November. Its lineup is made up of “80-90% award-winning films from Cannes, Berlin, Venice and Sundance,” according to Frederica, executive director of Jakarta World Cinema and director of KlikFilm, who oversees acquisitions.

	“We travel to [different] film markets, Berlin, Toronto, Cannes, etc.,” says Frederica, adding that the festival aims to bring the year’s most important art films to local audiences.

	This year’s edition has 102 theatrical titles, the most in the festival’s history, out of a total program of 207. Programming director Daniel Irawan says the goal for next year is to expand the lineup and keep working with its main venue, CGV Grand Indonesia, to increase audience capacity.

	Jakarta World Cinema also runs a short film competition, which took place in June and drew more than 300 entries from professionals, amateurs and students. All 30 competition titles and 20 non-competition titles on the shortlist will screen during the festival. The best short film and audience choice award winners will be announced on closing day, with the best short film winner receiving full funding from KlikFilm for the production and distribution of a debut feature.
	

	The festival is backed by Dana Indonesiaraya, a matching fund shared by the government and the film industry, according to Indonesian Culture Minister Fadli Zon. After the Jakarta edition closes on Nov. 7, the same program will travel to Bandung World Cinema and Malang World Cinema, two local extensions running Nov. 14–21.

schema.headline: Jakarta World Cinema Plans to Revive First Feature Competition With International Jury

title: Korea Box Office: Anime Hit ‘Chiikawa’ Retains Lead as Brad Pitt Thriller ‘Heart of the Beast’ Debuts
description: Japanese animated phenomenon “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” held the No. 1 position at the South Korean box office over the
body:
Japanese animated phenomenon “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” held the No. 1 position at the South Korean box office over the weekend of Oct. 30–Nov. 1, securing its third consecutive weekend atop the rankings. 

	According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council, the Toho-distributed fantasy release generated $1.7 million from 221,651 admissions across 1,167 screens, claiming 32.1% of the weekend market. Directed by Kei Oikawa and adapted from the popular manga by Nagano, the animated blockbuster has reached a cumulative gross of $20.1 million from 2,583,851 total admissions since its Sep. 30 rollout.
	

	Sony Pictures and TriStar’s survival thriller “Heart of the Beast” opened in second place, pulling in $1.2 million from 162,790 admissions across 1,106 screens to capture 23% of theatrical revenue. Since opening mid-week on Oct. 28, the title has accumulated $1.5 million from 215,237 admissions.

	By4M Studio and Barunson E&A’s workplace comedy “Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng” debuted in third place, taking in $326,609 from 44,799 admissions across 677 screens for 6.09% of the market. The directorial debut of screenwriter Lee Yong-jae stars Lee Sun-bin, Yoo Jae-myung, Kim Young-min, and Jeon Seok-ho, following a high school language teacher unexpectedly sequestered into the top-secret 40-day test-writing committee for the national college entrance examination. Following its premiere at the Busan International Film Festival and an Oct. 28 commercial bow, the comedy has grossed $505,208 from 71,767 viewers.
	

	Director Hur Jin-ho’s political crime thriller “The Assassin(s)” placed fourth in its sixth frame, collecting $307,719 from 41,265 admissions across 620 screens for 5.7% of receipts. Distributed by Hive Media Corp and starring Yu Hae-jin, Park Hae-il, and Lee Min-ho, the drama reconstructs the August 15, 1974 assassination attempt on President Park Chung-hee. Despite ongoing legal complaints and protests from conservative civic groups alleging historical distortion over its portrayal of state inquiry contradictions, the title lifted its cumulative total to $25.5 million from 3,448,036 admissions since its Sep. 23 launch.

	Anime re-release “Attack on Titan: Crimson Arrows” placed fifth, grossing $266,616 from 30,263 admissions across 233 screens. The theatrical re-issue of the 2014 feature pushed its updated cumulative haul to $547,187 from 72,324 admissions.

	CJ ENM’s gambling drama “Tazza: The Song of Beelzebub” took sixth place, earning $208,310 from 26,650 admissions across 498 screens. Directed by Choi Kook-hee and starring Byun Yo-han, Noh Jae-won, and Ayaka Miyoshi, the fourth installment in the comic-adapted franchise officially crossed the two-million-ticket threshold, reaching $15.7 million from 2,055,522 total viewers.

	CJ Entertainment’s psychological thriller “Paradise Lost,” directed by Yeon Sang-ho and starring Kim Hyun-joo and Bae Hyun-sung, placed seventh on the admissions chart with $124,104 from 17,053 admissions across 593 screens, bringing its cume to $1 million from 151,429 admissions.

	Warner Bros. and DC Studios’ “Clayface” placed eighth in admissions with 16,641 viewers across 444 screens, though it generated a higher revenue gross of $140,321. The film has accumulated $899,915 from 115,464 admissions.

	Universal’s tentpole “The Odyssey” took ninth place in its 13th weekend, adding $108,833 from 13,332 admissions across 254 screens. The film took 2.02% of the frame, lifting its cumulative total to $106.4 million from 12,335,377 admissions since its Aug. 5 opening.

	Rounding out the top ten, Japanese romantic drama “You, Like a Star” debuted with $77,264 from 10,091 admissions across 154 screens. Directed by Michihito Fujii and starring Ryusei Yokohama and Suzu Hirose as young lovers bound by shared hardship on an island in the Seto Inland Sea, the film has grossed $146,509 from 20,478 admissions since its Oct. 28 release.
	

	The overall market collective gross for the weekend was $5.3 million, down from last week’s $5.6 million.

schema.headline: Korea Box Office: Anime Hit ‘Chiikawa’ Retains Lead as Brad Pitt Thriller ‘Heart of the Beast’ Debuts

title: Palme d’Or Winner ‘Fjord’ Opens Jakarta World Cinema as Cinematographer Tudor Vladimir Panduru Leads Masterclass
description:
Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner “Fjord” opened the fifth edition of Jakarta World Cinema at CGV Grand Indonesia.

	Dan Adrian Bălănescu, Romani
body:
Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner “Fjord” opened the fifth edition of Jakarta World Cinema at CGV Grand Indonesia.

	Dan Adrian Bălănescu, Romania’s ambassador to Indonesia, said he was proud of the film, which is Romania’s submission for the international feature Oscar at the 2027 Academy Awards, and hoped it would speak to local audiences.

	“Many critics have criticized and accused the director, Cristian Mungiu, for, as they put it, flirting with conservative ideas. But at the same time, many critics have praised the film for being a courageous critique at the contemporary Western society,” Bălănescu said.
	

	The ambassador went on to cite a Romanian interview in which Mungiu said: “There’s no bravery in making a movie that defends progressive left-wing values. It’s outright provincial and opportunistic.”

	Tudor Vladimir Panduru, the film’s cinematographer and the festival’s sole masterclass guest, told the audience that “Fjord” marked his third collaboration with Mungiu after “Graduation” and “R.M.N.,” and the first they had shot outside Romania and in languages other than Romanian – English and Norwegian.

	“This film speaks about different values and perspectives in our world. So I think watching this film is important to answer a few questions for yourself, and to understand how to be a better person in the society we live in,” Panduru said.

	This year’s Jakarta World Cinema lineup features 207 titles, 102 of which are screening exclusively in theaters. Online streaming began Oct. 6 on KlikFilm. The lineup draws on 69 countries. Of the 207 titles, 120 have won awards at major festivals. Asian cinema accounts for 96 films, women directed 41, and 20 are official entries for the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards.
	

	The festival closes Nov. 7 with Thai horror film “Inherit.”

schema.headline: Palme d’Or Winner ‘Fjord’ Opens Jakarta World Cinema as Cinematographer Tudor Vladimir Panduru Leads Masterclass

title: From ‘The Devil Wears Prada’ to ‘The Invite,’ Costume Designers Shatter the Myth Behind Dressing Contemporary Characters: ‘It’s Very Difficult’
description: Contrary to popular belief, contemporary design in film is not just about shopping; it involves deep storytelling and thought behind how characters
body:
Contrary to popular belief, contemporary design in film is not just about shopping; it involves deep storytelling and thought behind how characters are dressed.

	Molly Rogers, who worked on “The Devil Wears Prada” as an assistant costume designer and was the sequel’s costume designer, said, “When someone comes up to me and says, ‘I really want to learn and work with you. I love to shop.’ That’s an automatic exit.”


	Rogers spoke at the Costume Design Roundtable at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, moderated by Variety’s Senior Artisans Editor Jazz Tangcay. Joining her were Ellen Mirojnick (“The Odyssey”), Arianne Phillips (“The Invite”), Linda Muir (“Werwulf”), Amy Roth (“I Play Rocky”) and Marci Rodgers (“Michael”).
	

	Mirojnick, known for her work on “Wall Street,” “Basic Instinct” and “Fatal Attraction,” discussed the challenges of contemporary costume design. “In the beginning of my career, I did a lot of contemporary costume, and I loved it. I loved being able to document what New York was like at that period, because yes, it was for film, but it also documented the history of what we were like, even if it was an elevated contemporary character.” She added, “Contemporary design is very difficult and very beautiful at the same time to create.”

	Rodgers recalled her first job on Spike Lee’s “She’s Gotta Have It.” Coming from Chicago, she knew New York’s style was different, so she asked Lee to sit with her during background casting. “So I could see how people are coming in here dressed.” When developing Nola Darling’s wardrobe, she learned the character’s favorite artist was Prince. “Purple is clearly going to be a thing. But it would be tidbits of purple. She wouldn’t shop at Saks.” Rodgers focused on thrift stores for Nola’s look. 
	

	On “Barbershop,” set in Chicago, she emphasized reflecting the community and fashion of the moment. Rodgers added, “A professor cautioned me that contemporary design would be the hardest thing I’d ever do. Actors will come in with an idea — or no idea — and then, after the table read, everything changes.”

	Phillips, whose credits include “Nocturnal Animals,” “The Invite” and “I Want Your Sex,” noted that contemporary design is often misunderstood. “I’ve been in rooms with studio executives. Directors, writers, producers and studio executives — they’re rich. They make a lot of money. They have a relationship to shopping, someone shopping for them. They can afford what they want, and they’re experts. This happens with actors a lot, where they’ll say, ‘Oh, I know my character wore those Prada boots.’ You have to be, as Marci said, a salesperson for your character. Costume design can be disrespected so easily by people sitting behind desks moving numbers around and not giving you the support you need.”

	Phillips also discussed the increasing influence of product placement in costume design as luxury brands enter the financing space. “We’re told by producers, ‘You have to use that product.’ You have to choose directors who support staying true to the story, as this is only going to get more complicated with how films are financed.”

	The designers also shared insights into their latest projects.

	Ellen Mirojnick crafted over 5,300 costumes for Christopher Nolan, focusing on Anne Hathaway’s Queen Penelope.

	The House of Ithaca’s color theme was burned red, which was reflected in Penelope’s costumes throughout the film. Mirojnick explained, “It was very important to keep her in those tones, not to disrupt the story.” 

	At the climactic moment when Odysseus returns, Penelope wears a blue dress that serves as her armor. “We created a drape with fine pleats, very tight and specific to the shape of her body. It went up through her neck, paired with a golden necklace — one of the only decorative pieces she wears. It felt as if she was ready for battle, and she was going to hold her own. She had a challenge to put forth, and her gown reinforced her strength.”

	Muir, who worked with Robert Eggers on “The Northman” and “Werwulf,” spoke about her meticulous research on wool, a commodity in Viking times that denoted wealth. Muir explained, “There are no wolves in the British Isles because the king ordered all of them eradicated so they wouldn’t eat the sheep.”
	

	The wealthy bought that wool, so anyone with a lot of wool clothing was upper class. Muir strove for authenticity but said, “The challenge with these films is finding people who can create wool fabrics, hats, jewelry, buttons, belts — all the things that make the whole picture when you have so few styles and elements to work with.”

	Phillips discussed her work with Olivia Wilde on “The Invite.” “It was my third time working with Olivia, so there’s a lot of trust there.”

	Phillips used only one costume change to set the tone. Cruz’s costume was layered intentionally to reveal more about her as the story progressed. Wilde’s Angela is a stay-at-home artist who had lost her creativity. Phillips said, “I worked with production designer Jade Healy to make sure she blended into the walls.” She continued, “I wanted Seth’s palette to be similar, and the blues were really bothering me because they weren’t in harmony. Then I realized that was perfect because the relationship is out of sync..”

	Rogers discussed the challenges of working on “The Devil Wears Prada 2.” “The first movie is so beloved, and I meditated on that for a while. It was a perfect storm — the script, the cast, the clothing. I thought, ‘OK, the curse of the sequel.’”

	But she pulled it off. She even brought back the iconic cerulean sweater because Andy (Anne Hathaway) would still have it after all these years.

	Rogers revealed, “Annie had scissors in her hands. I had wanted to shred it more naturally, like the sweater with holes in the elbows that you hang on to. But she chopped the sleeves off, and I realized it’s now a vest. I was trying to do menswear a little with her, so it read that way — it’s a vest.”

	Amy Roth reflected on “I Play Rocky.”

	She revealed the original “Rocky” film didn’t have a costume designer, so there were no references to pull from. She said, “Recreating this iconic look — not just from the film, but from my memory and everybody’s collective memory of Rocky — the hat, the leather jacket, the gloves, the bouncing ball, they were all crucial.”

	Roth explained that the leather jacket was so important. “We had to make it and age it. I found the original jacket on eBay, in my actor’s size and felt relief.”
	

	She credits actor Anthony Ippolito for elevating the work and her work. “He wanted his body to look exactly like Stallone’s. He posed like Stallone. He just embodied his body. He really wanted to do what we were doing. He would bring pictures of things he wore, and we’d recreate them for him.”

	Rogers also touched upon her work on “Michael” and recreating the “Thriller” video. She said, “It was one of the last things we shot. I had a research book of 800 pages, and Deborah Landis told me something interesting. We all know the leather jacket is iconic, but she revealed that Michael’s Levi jeans were originally white and she had to dye them red.”

	Levi’s collaborated with the filmmakers, sending a few pairs to recreate the look. “I had a Pantone book and recreated the beaded jacket, realizing there were two different shades of red — color value is so important,” she said.

	It was all about capturing every detail, and the zombie dancers mattered just as much. “I thought, ‘That’s the woman in the pink dress. I’ve got to put the pearls right here.”

	Watch the full conversation below.

schema.headline: From ‘The Devil Wears Prada’ to ‘The Invite,’ Costume Designers Shatter the Myth Behind Dressing Contemporary Characters: ‘It’s Very Difficult’

title: Dave Bautista Reveals He’s Gained 20 Pounds of Muscle Ahead of Playing Kratos in ‘God of War’ Series
description: Dave Bautista is once again showing off his muscle gains ahead of stepping into the role of Kratos for the highly anticipated “God of War” series.
body:
Dave Bautista is once again showing off his muscle gains ahead of stepping into the role of Kratos for the highly anticipated “God of War” series. The “Guardians of the Galaxy” actor last gave fans a glimpse into his transformation two months ago, saying he’d begun weight training again but still had time “to get to where I need to be.”

	This time, Bautista shared a video on his Instagram story with the text “Gained 20 lbs for GOW” and a “250” sticker, indicating his current weight. Fittingly, the actor is wearing a “God of War” T-shirt in the post.
	

	In August, Bautista signed on to play Kratos, replacing Ryan Hurst, who was originally cast and suffered an on-set injury that led Prime Video to replace him. (Hurst tore his bicep on set and required surgery that would have delayed production into 2027.) Filming began in Vancouver in February, but the production will have to reshoot all scenes with Hurst using Bautista.

	The series will follow the story of the two most recent “God of War” video games, which follow Kratos as he raises his ten-year-old son Atreus (Callum Vinson) while battling gods of the Norse pantheon. Per the logline, “Father and son Kratos and Atreus embark on a journey to spread the ashes of their wife and mother, Faye. Through their adventures, Kratos tries to teach his son to be a better god, while Atreus tries to teach his father how to be a better human.”

	Prime Video gave “God of War” a two-season order, with the two seasons set to shoot back-to-back.

	Bautista has starred in films including “My Spy,” “Knock at the Cabin,” “The Wrecking Crew” and more. He will next appear in “Road House 2” and the “Highlander” reboot.

            Rising fitness influencer Khiana Smith remains hospitalized in the ICU after suffering a brain infection ... and admits she feels "absolutely helpless."
      
    
            Taking to TikTok ... Khiana said that she has been "bedbound in ICU in Bali with a brain infection that could have killed me."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The influencer -- who boasts nearly 87,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram -- said that she contracted bacterial meningitis and has since been diagnosed with pneumonia during her Bali trip.
      

            What started as a headache turned into "extreme head pains, dizziness, slurred speech, slurred vision, and a severe sensitivity to light."
      
    
            After spending 9 days in the ICU, Khiana said she "lost a lot of memory, like, I really struggle to remember things."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As she remains hospital-bound, Khiana added ... "I feel absolutely helpless, and I just wanna go home."
      
    
            Rest up, Khiana!

title: Legendary 'Miracle' Mets Player Jerry Koosman Dead 83
description:
N.Y. Mets Legend
                          Jerry Koosman Dead
body:
N.Y. Mets Legend
                          Jerry Koosman Dead
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Jerry Koosman -- who played on the 1969 "Miracle" Mets team that won the World Series -- has died ... the team announced.
      
    
            Koosman passed away surrounded by family in Osceola, Wisconsin ... the Mets shared on the team's Medium account.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            According to the team ... Jerry had battled multiple illnesses before his death.
      

            The pitcher won Game 2 of the '69 World Series ... before topping it off with the Game 5 W that clinched the series for the team.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jerry's teammate Ron Swoboda spoke out about his death ... "Jerry was our protector. Any time the opposition threw at our guys, Jerry took care of it."
      
    
            In addition to his '69 World Series title ... Jerry also boasted 2 All-Star appearances.
      
    
            Jerry was 83.
      
    
            RIP

title: NJ 5th Grade Teacher, Accused of Having 11-Year-Old Student's Baby, Pleads Guilty
description:
NJ Teacher
                          Accused of Having 11-Year-Old Student's Baby
body:
NJ Teacher
                          Accused of Having 11-Year-Old Student's Baby
                          Pleads Guilty
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                November 1, 2026
                
                            12:48 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 1, 2026
                                2:39 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Laura Caron -- a 36-year-old former 5th grade teacher -- has pleaded guilty to one of the charges against her ... after being accused of sexually assaulting a student and having his baby.
      
    
            Caron -- who was charged in January 2025 -- was accused of abusing her victim as early as 11 years old ... PEOPLE reported.
      
    
            Prosecutors claimed the abuse lasted for 4 years ... and a probable cause affidavit obtained by the outlet claimed she became pregnant with and gave birth to his child.
      

            She was 27 at the time ... he was only 13.
      
    
            Caron pleaded guilty to second-degree endangering the welfare of a child with sexual conduct.
      
    
            As part of her plea ... Caron will not only forfeit her teacher's license, she's set to receive a 5-year sentence, although her sentencing hearing will take place in January.
      
    
            The Cape May County Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement ... "Before Caron serves her State Prison sentence, she will be evaluated at the Adult Diagnostic and Treatment Center at Avenel for classification to determine whether she is deemed repetitive and/or compulsive which could impact her sentence."
      
    
            After serving her sentence ... Caron will also be subject to parole supervision for the rest of her life and have to register as sex offender.

title: 'Bachelor' Alum Melissa Rycroft Arrested For DWI
description:
'Bachelor' Alum Melissa Rycroft
                          Arrested for 2nd DWI Months After Plead
body:
'Bachelor' Alum Melissa Rycroft
                          Arrested for 2nd DWI Months After Pleading Guilty to First
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Melissa Rycroft has been charged with her second DWI just months after pleading to her first ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The former 'Bachelor' star was charged with driving while intoxicated, driving while license was invalid with a prior conviction or suspension without financial responsibility, and collision causing damage to a vehicle under $200.
      
    
            She was arrested and booked Sunday ... according to Tarrant County jail records.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As part of her August sentencing for her 2025 DWI ... she received 20 months of probation and was ordered to pay roughly $2,000 in fines and court costs.
      
    
            In addition to 36 hours of community service, she was ordered to finish a DWI education course, and participate in a substance abuse evaluation.
      
    
            Her plea deal also mentioned she couldn't drink or use drugs while on probation ... we'll keep you posted as we learn more about this latest alleged DWI.
